title: LAD occlusion ('widow-maker')
text: The anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery supplies the anterior left ventricle, the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum and the apex. It is the most common site of coronary occlusion. Proximal occlusion causes a large anterior infarction (ST elevation V1-V4) with risk of cardiogenic shock, left ventricular aneurysm and mural thrombus, and septal rupture. A left main stem stenosis threatens both the LAD and circumflex territories.

targets: Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle
title: Right coronary occlusion and conduction block
text: In most people (right-dominant circulation) the right coronary artery gives the posterior interventricular artery and supplies the sinoatrial node (about 60%) and atrioventricular node (about 80%). Inferior infarction (ST elevation II, III, aVF) therefore commonly causes sinus bradycardia and AV block, and can involve the right ventricle (hypotension with clear lungs; nitrates are dangerous) and the posteromedial papillary muscle, whose single blood supply makes it prone to rupture and acute mitral regurgitation.

title: Circumflex occlusion
text: Supplies the lateral and posterior left ventricle and, in left-dominant hearts, the posterior interventricular artery. Circumflex infarcts are the 'electrically silent' ones: ST elevation may be absent on a standard 12-lead ECG, showing only as ST depression in V1-V3 (posterior infarct), so they are easily missed.

targets: Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve
title: Mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation
text:
Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic: fused commissures raise left atrial pressure, dilating the atrium (atrial fibrillation, thrombus and stroke), causing pulmonary hypertension, haemoptysis, and hoarseness when the enlarged atrium stretches the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner syndrome). Opening snap and mid-diastolic rumble at the apex.
Mitral regurgitation results from prolapse (myxomatous degeneration), papillary muscle rupture after infarction, chordal rupture, endocarditis or ventricular dilatation; a pansystolic murmur radiates to the axilla.

title: Aortic stenosis and regurgitation
text:
Calcific stenosis of a tricuspid valve in the elderly, or earlier in a congenitally bicuspid valve, causes the triad of angina, exertional syncope and heart failure, an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse. Left ventricular hypertrophy follows; microangiopathic shear can cause GI bleeding from angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome).
Regurgitation (aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome or syphilis, endocarditis, bicuspid valve) produces a collapsing pulse and early diastolic murmur.

targets: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
title: Tricuspid endocarditis
text: Right-sided endocarditis of the tricuspid valve is characteristic of intravenous drug use, typically with Staphylococcus aureus. Septic emboli go to the lungs, causing multiple cavitating pulmonary nodules rather than the systemic emboli of left-sided endocarditis. Carcinoid syndrome with liver metastases causes fibrosis of the tricuspid and pulmonary valves.

title: Cardiac tamponade and pericarditis
text:
The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch acutely, so even 100-200 mL of rapidly accumulating blood (trauma, ventricular free wall rupture, aortic dissection) compresses the heart: Beck triad of hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds, plus pulsus paradoxus. Pericardiocentesis is performed from the subxiphoid angle.
Pericarditis causes sharp chest pain eased by sitting forward, referred to the shoulder via the phrenic nerve, a friction rub and widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation. Chronic constrictive pericarditis (tuberculosis) produces Kussmaul sign.

title: Septal defects and paradoxical embolism
text:
Ventricular septal defects are the commonest congenital heart lesion, usually in the membranous septum, producing a harsh pansystolic murmur. Atrial septal defects (secundum type most often) and a patent foramen ovale allow venous thrombi to cross to the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolism and stroke), especially during Valsalva.
Uncorrected large left-to-right shunts cause pulmonary hypertension that can eventually reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome) with cyanosis and clubbing.

title: Aortic dissection and traumatic rupture
text:
An intimal tear lets blood split the media, usually from hypertension, Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, bicuspid valve or cocaine. Tearing chest pain radiating to the back, unequal arm blood pressures and a widened mediastinum. Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency (tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary or carotid occlusion); type B begins distal to the left subclavian artery and is usually managed medically.
Rapid deceleration tears the aorta at the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery where the ligamentum arteriosum tethers it. Coarctation typically occurs at the same site, causing rib notching from dilated intercostal collaterals and radiofemoral delay.

title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
text:
Usually infrarenal, in older male smokers with atherosclerosis. Most are asymptomatic and found on screening as a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus. Rupture into the retroperitoneum causes abdominal or back pain, hypotension and flank bruising; it is often misdiagnosed as renal colic. Elective repair is offered from about 5.5 cm. Complications include distal embolism, aortocaval and aortoenteric fistula (especially after graft repair).
Mesenteric ischaemia and Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion: buttock claudication, impotence, absent femoral pulses) are other aortic pathologies here.

title: Aspiration and lung cancer location
text:
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies and aspiration usually go to the right lung: the posterior segment of the upper lobe and superior segment of the lower lobe when supine, and the basal segments when upright.
Squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are typically central (hilar); adenocarcinoma is peripheral and the commonest type in non-smokers. Small cell carcinoma causes paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, ACTH, Lambert-Eaton). Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumours at the apex invade the brachial plexus, stellate ganglion (Horner syndrome) and subclavian vessels.

title: Pneumothorax and pleural effusion
text:
Spontaneous pneumothorax results from rupture of apical subpleural blebs in tall thin young men; secondary pneumothorax complicates COPD. A tension pneumothorax, where a one-way valve traps air, shifts the mediastinum, kinks the great veins and causes obstructive shock; decompression is needed immediately (2nd intercostal space midclavicular line, or 4th-5th space in the midaxillary line).
Chest drains are inserted in the 'triangle of safety' just above a rib, to avoid the intercostal vein, artery and nerve running in the costal groove. Fluid gathers first in the costodiaphragmatic recess. The parietal pleura is sensitive to pain (intercostal and phrenic nerves), the visceral pleura is not.

title: Tracheal intubation, tracheostomy and stenosis
text:
An endotracheal tube passed too far usually enters the right main bronchus, collapsing the left lung. The carina lies at about T4/T5 (sternal angle); a widened carinal angle suggests enlarged subcarinal nodes or left atrial enlargement.
Tracheostomy is performed through the 2nd-4th rings, below the thyroid isthmus; hazards include the inferior thyroid veins, a thyroid ima artery and the brachiocephalic artery (tracheo-innominate fistula). Prolonged cuff pressure causes ischaemic tracheal stenosis. Tracheomalacia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia are congenital anomalies.

title: Diaphragmatic hernias and phrenic nerve palsy
text:
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia, usually a posterolateral left Bochdalek defect from failed closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane, lets bowel into the thorax, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and neonatal respiratory distress. Morgagni hernias are anterior and retrosternal.
Traumatic rupture is more often left-sided (the liver protects the right). Phrenic nerve palsy (C3-C5; tumours, cardiac surgery, cervical trauma) causes paradoxical upward movement of the hemidiaphragm on sniffing. Irritation of central diaphragmatic peritoneum refers pain to the shoulder tip.

title: Thymoma and myasthenia gravis
text:
Thymomas are anterior mediastinal tumours, one of the 'four Ts' (thymus, teratoma, thyroid, 'terrible' lymphoma). About a third of patients with thymoma have myasthenia gravis, and thymic hyperplasia is common in younger myasthenic patients; thymectomy improves the disease. Thymomas are also associated with pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia (Good syndrome).
Thymic aplasia in DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) causes T-cell immunodeficiency along with hypocalcaemia and conotruncal heart defects.

title: Chylothorax
text: The thoracic duct ascends on the right of the oesophagus, crosses to the left at about T5 and drains into the left venous angle. Injury during oesophagectomy, thoracic spine surgery or central line insertion, or obstruction by lymphoma, leaks milky, triglyceride-rich chyle into the pleural cavity: right-sided if below T5, left-sided if above. Prolonged leaks cause malnutrition and lymphopenia.

title: Azygos collateral pathway
text: The azygos system connects the superior and inferior venae cavae. When the SVC is obstructed below the azygos entry, or the IVC is obstructed, blood returns through azygos and hemiazygos veins, which dilate. The azygos vein also receives oesophageal veins, forming the systemic side of the oesophageal portosystemic anastomosis. An azygos lobe is a normal variant where the vein is trapped in a pleural fissure of the right upper lobe.

title: Superior vena cava syndrome
text: Compression of the thin-walled SVC by a right upper lobe bronchogenic carcinoma (especially small cell), lymphoma or mediastinal nodes, or thrombosis around central lines, causes facial plethora and swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins, and headache worse on bending forward. Raising the arms may produce facial congestion (Pemberton sign). Airway compression makes it an oncological emergency.

title: IVC filters and Budd-Chiari syndrome
text:
Filters placed in the infrarenal IVC trap lower limb emboli when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (hepatic vein or suprahepatic IVC thrombosis in polycythaemia vera, pregnancy, the contraceptive pill) causes Budd-Chiari syndrome: painful hepatomegaly, ascites and congestive 'nutmeg' liver. Enlargement of the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC, is typical.

title: Pulmonary embolism
text: Deep venous thrombi from the legs or pelvis travel through the right heart to the pulmonary arteries. A large 'saddle' embolus across the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk causes acute right ventricular failure, hypotension and sudden death. Smaller emboli cause pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and wedge-shaped peripheral infarcts, which are uncommon because of the dual bronchial supply. Classic ECG pattern: sinus tachycardia, right heart strain, S1Q3T3.

title: Sternal fracture and sternotomy
text:
Direct steering-wheel or seat-belt impact fractures the sternum and should raise suspicion of blunt cardiac injury. The sternal angle marks T4/T5: the 2nd costal cartilage, tracheal bifurcation, beginning and end of the aortic arch and the division between superior and inferior mediastinum.
Median sternotomy is the standard cardiac surgical approach; deep sternal wound infection and mediastinitis are serious complications. A sternal foramen (failed fusion) is a hazard during sternal marrow aspiration.
